3886070616239448163.text:
I’m a psychologist.
Here are the 25 wisest pieces of dating advice I’ve ever heard…

3886070674800347926.text:
1. If you regularly feel confused, anxious, or unsure about where you stand with someone, that uncertainty is a form of inner wisdom.

Listen to it.

People who are interested in you and have the capacity to love you well will bring you clarity.

Those who lack interest or capacity will bring you confusion, uncertainty, and anxiety.

3886070748838225510.text:
2. Your greatest power is your willingness to walk away.

Walking away from the wrong person is how you commit to your own standards and self-love.

The moment you become too attached to a specific outcome, and too afraid to walk away, you give away your agency.

3886070813942165641.text:
3. It’s hard to be interesting to someone until they're already interested in you.

No amount of wit, charm, or effort will manufacture attraction that isn't there.

Don't exhaust yourself performing for an audience who never showed up for you.

4031861687477342101.text:
As a psychologist, I can't emphasize this enough:

You can care deeply about someone and still recognize that being with them isn’t good for you.

Let me explain:

4031861711040952352.text: How much you care about someone tells you how much empathy you have for them. It doesn’t tell you whether a relationship with them meets your needs, aligns with your values, or supports the life you want to build.

4031861738454917671.text: Caring about someone and being compatible with them are two entirely different things. Caring comes from attachment; compatibility comes from alignment.

4031861765223020200.text: People get stuck in relationships when they assume that they’re deeply aligned with their partner simply because they’re deeply attached to them.

4028972693839649642.text:
Dating burnout is real.

Psychology helps explain why it hurts so much:

4028972726160938526.text:
In dating, burnout happens when you get your hopes up about someone new, only to be let down—time and time again.

Here are 3 reasons why that drains the life out of you:

4028972764379427343.text:
1. Repeatedly getting your hopes up is exhausting.

Every promising connection brings a little excitement. You start looking forward to their texts, imagining your next date, and wondering what a future together might look like.

When things end, you’re not just losing the person. You’re also losing the future you imagined with them.

That forces you to suddenly experience two kinds of grief: the loss of connection and the loss of hope. Both hurt in their own way.

4028972803973659705.text:
2. Vulnerability without long-term intimacy takes an emotional toll.

Getting to know someone takes vulnerability. You share stories about your childhood, explain what matters to you, invest time and effort, and gradually build familiarity.

Then, when things don’t work out, you have to start that entire process again with someone new. Back to square one.

After repeating that cycle enough times, the thought of another first date can feel draining and pointless.

4027506189143102057.text:
As a psychologist, I can't stress this enough:

Being single and having strong friendships is so much healthier than being in a strong relationship but having weak friendships.

4027506219727952203.text: Romantic relationships are important and often highly fulfilling, yes. But they shouldn't be the only source of love, connection, and emotional support in our lives.

4027506257459897304.text:
Even a wonderful romantic relationship can't fulfill every emotional and social need we have. When we neglect our friendships in favor of a partner, we risk placing too much pressure on one person to be our entire support system.

And if that relationship ends, we find ourselves without the reliable platonic connections that could help us heal.

4027506297221932448.text: I think we should all strive to build a life so rich in friendship that a romantic connection adds to our happiness rather than becoming its sole foundation.

4026815358266442376.text:
There’s a scientific reason why many people get more attached to someone who’s inconsistent than to someone shows reliable interest in them.

It’s called “intermittent reinforcement.”

And it goes like this:

4026815391955133659.text:
Imagine dating two people.

The first person texts you regularly, makes plans, and follows through. You don’t spend much time wondering where you stand with them.

The second person does the opposite. They’re inconsistent. Some days, text you a lot, compliment you, and make you feel like the most desirable person in the world. Other days, they barely acknowledge your existence.

4026815421877264879.text:
Unfortunately, in the short term, most people will be more drawn to the second person (the inconsistent partner) than the first (the consistent one).

This is an unfortunate reality of just how we’re wired psychologically.

4026815457939941194.text:
This happens not because you like the inconsistent person more, but because their inconsistency creates a problem your mind desperately wants to solve:

Why were they so affectionate yesterday but distant today? Did I say something wrong? Are they losing interest in me? What can I do to win them back?

4023902805869678852.text:
It is simply impossible to build a healthy relationship with a narcissist.

Psychology helps explain why:

4023902842737628430.text:
A healthy relationship needs two people who can recognize that each other's feelings, needs, and perspectives matter, even when they don't agree.

Narcissists aren’t able to do that.

4023902891366404319.text:
Narcissists have a deep need to protect their ego. When you tell a narcissist they hurt you, they treat your pain like an accusation they need to defeat rather than an experience they want to understand.

When you establish a boundary, they interpret it as disrespect.

When you ask for accountability, they turn the conversation into an argument about why you're the problem.

4023902927428989438.text:
Over time, when you’re with a narcissist, you start managing their reactions. You learn which subjects to avoid. You rehearse how to bring up concerns. You apologize to restore peace, even when you were the person who got hurt.

Gradually, the relationship becomes less about two people's needs and more about protecting one person's ego.

4023255869599898753.text:
A psychologist’s guide: HOW TO LOVE BOMB SOMEONE

(revealing the signs so you know how to avoid getting love bombed yourself)

4023255905217899603.text:
STEP 1: Make them feel like you’re their soulmate.

Tell them you've never felt this way about anyone before. Say they're different from everyone else you've dated. Make them feel like your connection is something that happens once in a lifetime.

And make sure you do all of this before you've actually gotten to know them.

4023255971169147321.text:
STEP 3: Make big promises about the future.

Talk about vacations you'll take together. Introduce the possibility of moving in. Tell them you can see yourself marrying them someday.

Don't worry about whether you're actually prepared to follow through.

Remember: You're selling them a future, not building one.

4023256005243679244.text:
STEP 4: Keep this up for 3-4 weeks, maybe even a few months if you have it in you.

No matter what, remember that it’s your duty to make them feel incredibly loved as soon as possible.

Show them how amazing you are and how special your connection is by whatever means necessary.

4023189222738481378.text:
I’m a psychologist, and I’ve seen a lot of relationships fall apart because people avoid hard conversations.

Here’s the blunt reality:

4023189249170984209.text: Some people use silence as a punishment in relationships. They shut down to gain control or withdraw to prove a point. But the only point they’re proving is their emotional immaturity. Mature partners communicate. Immature partners disappear.

4027563562952210559.parentText: It's not either or. My experience is that people with strong marriages often also have healthy friendships.

4005769361562257123.text: She was shocked and replayed everything from the past 7 months. She wondered: Was she too eager? Too available? Too much? Not enough? During the breakup, he had even told her “You did nothing wrong, this is just about how I feel” but that didn’t stop her from spiraling. She told me “If apparently I didn’t even do anything wrong and someone STILL doesn’t even want to be with me, what does that say about me?”

4005150471487586433.text: Someone can mean what they say in the moment and still be inconsistent over time. The truth is that anyone can say the right thing in the right moment. How someone acts consistently is where their real character and capacity live. This is why actions speak louder than words.

4002840882538232889.text: "Every night this retreat, I sat and watched the sunset. It was beautiful. But it made me sad because I started to wonder: How many sunsets in my life have I missed because I was too damn busy to stop and look?"

4001522596986160963.text: He texted her every morning before work and called her at night. He sent her Google maps links to restaurants he wanted to take her to, talked about a weekend trip they should plan, and joked about what neighborhood they would live in “when we move in together.” She laughed and told him they barely knew each other, to which he replied “I mean it. I haven't felt this way with anyone before.”

4001506113472155100.text:
1. They pursue hardest when there’s still distance between you.

They may be incredibly attentive while they’re trying to win you over.

But once they know you’re attached, the energy shifts from pursuit to retreat.

1. You will sometimes be rejected by people you desperately wanted.

You will sometimes reject wonderful people who desperately wanted you.

Both experiences teach the same lesson: good character alone does not create compatibility.

3990757317478212901.text:
Sometimes the question isn’t “Is this relationship unhealthy?”

It’s “Is this relationship giving me enough of what I want love to actually feel like?”

Absence of dysfunction and presence of fulfillment are two different standards.

3987028156900928732.text:
I’d started dabbling in stand-up comedy only a few months earlier and was frankly shocked that the judges had voted me through.

I didn’t enter the contest looking to win; I just wanted to challenge myself to do something out of my comfort zone.

And out of my comfort zone I sure was—a PhD nerd with almost no performing experience, attempting to make a room of 200 strangers laugh.

3986921937964077322.text:
Confidence is not the ability to command a room.

Sometimes it’s the ability to enter one without believing you need to become someone else first.

If someone keeps you close but never commits, that’s a red flag.

Even if they call it “taking it slow,” it’s likely either avoidance or disinterest.

Either way, that’s a person who likes having access without taking responsibility.

3981862848699514592.text:
Emotional capacity is holding space for someone else’s feelings.

If someone makes everything about them, they don’t have space for you.

It’s not your job to squeeze into smaller spaces. It’s your job to walk away from spaces that aren’t enough.
